zones.label: Out Through the Window
zones.summary: Pasting into a hosted model sends documents out of the lab to a provider's computers. Once sent, a disclosure to a third party cannot be undone.
facts: Unpublished results are not secret in a legal sense, but placing them in a hosted AI tool is a disclosure to a third party under that provider's terms (Chapter 18).

Ask of any hosted tool: may inputs train models, how long are they kept and who can see them, where are they processed, and do your institution's contract terms differ from consumer terms (Chapter 18).
A disclosure cannot be undone. Classify before you paste, and if you are unsure, use the local model or ask first (Chapter 18).
A cloud agent computer means your files and sessions live on someone else's hardware (Chapter 19).

zones.label: The Cloud End
zones.summary: At the far end, what happens to your inputs depends on the provider's terms: how long they are kept, who sees them, and whether they train models.
facts: Agent data exposure is what happens to data you give an agent: training use, retention, who can see it, where it is processed, and whether memory can be inspected and deleted (Chapter 19).
Defaults differ. At least one personal-agent product trains on user data by default, with an opt-out (Chapter 19).
For one early-beta product, the research notes record that retention defaults, credential handling, and audit records are undocumented (Chapter 19).
Where the answers about a hosted tool are not satisfactory, a local open-weight model keeps the data on your machine (Chapter 18).

zones.label: Inside the Lab Boundary
zones.summary: A model you run on a rack in your own lab keeps the documents inside the dashed boundary. You decide where data go and what the agent can reach.
facts: A self-hosted agent runs on a machine you control: a laptop, a server, or your own cloud account (Chapter 19).
You gain control over where the data go and what the agent can reach (Chapter 19).
A local open-weight model keeps data on your machine (Chapter 18).
Keep the master knowledge graph where you control it and give agents views of it, so the agent's memory is a copy that can be discarded (Chapter 19).

zones.label: You Maintain It
zones.summary: Running your own model buys control and costs work: setup, security, and upkeep fall to you, along with the energy the hardware uses.
facts: A self-hosted agent gives you control and also puts setup, security, and maintenance on you (Chapter 19).
With an open-source self-hosted agent, you manage your own servers, secrets, and security (Chapter 19).
Reviews recorded in the chapter's notes report runaway loops, malicious skills, and unattended deletions for one self-hosted agent (Chapter 19).
Environmental cost is real and rarely visible to the user. Use the smallest model that does the job and avoid loops and sweeps that nobody will read (Chapter 18).

zones.label: Green Lane
zones.summary: Public material may go to any tool. In the illustrative four-class policy this is class 0.
facts: Class 0, public: published papers, public datasets, and open-source code may be given to any tool (Chapter 18).
In Chapter 18's sorter exercise, a published IEEE paper and an open-source simulation script from a public repository are both class 0.
The classification is illustrative. A group needs a small one that people can apply without looking it up, with a rule for what each class may be given to (Chapter 18).
The poster's three lanes simplify the four classes of Chapter 18: public, needs a decision, never to a hosted tool.

zones.label: Yellow Lane
zones.summary: Internal and unpublished material needs a decision first: an approved tool, a local model, or your advisor's written approval.
facts: Class 1, internal: lab notes on setup, scripts, and draft text without new results may go to an approved hosted tool or a local model (Chapter 18).
Class 2, unpublished: unpublished measurements and designs may go to a local model, or to a hosted tool with the advisor's written approval (Chapter 18).
A new circuit netlist that has not been published or filed is class 2, because disclosure may affect later protection (Chapter 18).
An item that falls in two classes takes the more restrictive one (Chapter 18).

zones.label: Red Lane
zones.summary: Obligated data stays off hosted tools: data under NDA, export-controlled data, participants' personal data, and licensed vendor files.
facts: Class 3, obligated: data under NDA, export-controlled technical data, personal data of participants, and vendor files under license (Chapter 18).
These go to a local model only, and only if the agreement allows. Otherwise they go to no AI tool (Chapter 18).
In electrical engineering, process design kits and device models are usually restricted (Chapter 18).
Interview transcripts with identifiable participants are class 3, governed by the consent and ethics approval (Chapter 18).

zones.label: The Lab Policy Sheet
zones.summary: A one-page lab AI policy turns these principles into rules that a new student can follow on the first day.
facts: A lab AI policy is a short written statement of how a research group uses AI tools. One page is enough (Chapter 18).
Its skeleton has eight sections: purpose, accountability, data classes and tools, disclosure, verification, approved tools, skills and training, and review (Chapter 18).
Keep it as a Markdown file in the group's repository and link it from each project's AGENTS.md, so agents read it at the start of every session (Chapter 18).
Review it every six months and whenever a venue or institution changes its rules. Chapter 18 is not legal advice, so check your own institution's current rules.

quiz.question: A student pastes unpublished ENOB measurements into a chat assistant to save time. Which region shows where those inputs travel and why the paste cannot be taken back?
quiz.explanation: Placing unpublished results in a hosted tool is a disclosure to a third party, and a disclosure cannot be undone.

quiz.question: Before adopting a hosted assistant you must ask whether it may train on your inputs and how long it keeps them. Which region shows where those answers play out?
quiz.explanation: Training use, retention, who can see the data, and where it is processed are decided by the provider's terms and defaults.

quiz.question: A personal agent product trains on user data by default and you must opt out. Which region shows the kind of exposure this creates?
quiz.explanation: Agent data exposure covers training use and retention at the provider, and defaults differ between products.

quiz.question: Your group wants its documents never to leave the building. Which region shows the setup that gives that control?
quiz.explanation: A self-hosted or local model runs on a machine you control, so you decide where the data go and what the agent reaches.

quiz.question: A lab runs its own model. Someone must patch it, protect its secrets, and watch for runaway loops. Which region shows this burden?
quiz.explanation: Self-hosting trades convenience for control: setup, security, and maintenance become the lab's job.

quiz.question: A published IEEE paper and an open-source script from a public repository need summarizing. Which region shows where they may go?
quiz.explanation: Class 0 public material may be given to any tool.

quiz.question: A new circuit netlist has not been published or filed. Using a hosted tool needs the advisor's written approval, or a local model. Which region shows this?
quiz.explanation: Unpublished designs are class 2 and need a decision before they go to any tool.

quiz.question: Foundry model files under NDA and identifiable interview transcripts are in the folder. Which region shows where they belong?
quiz.explanation: Obligated data goes to a local model only, and only if the agreement allows, or else to no AI tool.

quiz.question: A new student asks on the first day what the group's rules for AI tools are. Which region shows the single page that answers?
quiz.explanation: A one-page lab AI policy sets data classes, disclosure, verification, and approved tools in advance.
